replies.author: @GameAnGrog
replies.text:
My grandmother was a compulsive spender and hoarder.  She spent all her free time watching the shopping network and buying  QVC garbage.  We tried to help her stop, and she responded with cruelty, and disowning the entire family.  By the time she passed away, she had spent more than $1.7 million dollars and was even using my mentally disabled uncles disability checks to feed her shopping addiction.

The collective savings and smart investing of my great grandparents, my grandfather, her 3 siblings, and my grandfathers 5 siblings was entirely spent, while she had never held a job in her life.

Instead of that accumulated wealth passing on to her kids and eventually us grandkids, we were instead left sharing tens of thousands of dollars of debt.

It took decades, and a life time of hardwork from more than a dozen people to build that up, and in the end, the sum of the work of multiple generations was wiped out with nothing to show for it because one person couldn't make smart financial decisions.

comments.author: @WaddleQwacker
comments.text:
Random info dump: the word “mortgage” comes from old French, formed by combining “mort” (dead) and “gage” (pledge). Literally, it means “dead pledge” and was most popular in the middle age I think.
It has not been used anymore in modern French for at least the last two centuries in favor of other technical words. Idk what it precisely means in the USA today, but historically, the “pledge” referred to the property used as security for a loan, and the “dead” aspect referred to the final outcome of that pledge: either the debt was fully repaid (the pledge was “released,” and the agreement ended), or the borrower defaulted (the pledge was “dead” to them, and the lender took ownership of the property). In both cases, the pledge’s fate was sealed. Hence, “dead.”
